error_modes.label: Takeoff airspeed control and rotation point

texts.0: SP, due to an imprecise power application and a late reference to the calculated takeoff data, did not execute the T/O with the standard airspeed. Rotation was withheld well past the computed point and the aircraft was flown off more than 10 knots above the standard takeoff airspeed, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance. The fast condition was not recognized and the acceleration continued unchecked. IP intervened with a directive call to rotate and set the takeoff attitude before the remaining runway became a factor.
texts.1: SP, due to a hesitant rotation input at the computed speed, did not execute the T/O with the standard airspeed. Liftoff occurred about 10 knots fast, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance. SP made no corrective input until the IP gave a verbal call, and the airspeed was brought back to the standard only after that prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed cross-check of the airspeed indication in the last part of the ground roll, did not rotate exactly at the standard takeoff airspeed. Liftoff occurred approximately 7 knots fast, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances. SP recognized the fast trend, set the takeoff attitude and contained the airspeed in time, with no IP intervention required.
texts.3: SP executed the T/O with the standard airspeed, cross-checking the airspeed indication against the calculated takeoff data throughout the ground roll. Rotation was initiated at the briefed speed and the airspeed at liftoff remained within the -0,+5 knots tolerance. Control inputs were smooth and no acceleration overshoot developed.
texts.4: SP executed the T/O with the standard airspeed and rotated precisely at the computed speed. Airspeed at liftoff showed negligible deviation from the standard takeoff airspeed, with no perceptible overshoot during the acceleration. The airspeed cross-check was continuous from brake release to liftoff and the calculated takeoff data were verified against actual aircraft performance.
texts.marginal: SP executed the T/O within the required airspeed tolerance, but rotation was consistently initiated a few knots late and the airspeed trended toward the upper edge of the standard on each attempt. No prompting was needed and every takeoff stayed within standards. SP is expected to tighten the airspeed cross-check in the final part of the ground roll so that rotation is initiated at the exact standard takeoff airspeed.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the rotation speed as the computed value approached and demonstrating the backpressure to apply, SP rotated on the call given. The cross-check of the airspeed indication through the ground roll has not yet been established, so the computed rotation speed is still confirmed by the IP rather than read independently. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin cross-checking the airspeed indication through the roll without the rotation speed being called.
texts_at.1: SP made no corrective input on the rotation speed until the IP gave a verbal call, then brought liftoff back to about 10 knots fast, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance, because the cross-check of the airspeed indication had not been established before the computed speed arrived. Rotation itself was made at the correct point once the call had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to establish the cross-check earlier so liftoff does not need the IP's call.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a fast trend from a delayed cross-check late in the ground roll, set the takeoff attitude and contained liftoff to approximately 7 knots fast, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, without any IP intervention. The correction was made in time to avoid a further acceleration overshoot. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to establish the cross-check earlier in the ground roll so the trend does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP executed the T/O with the standard airspeed, cross-checking the airspeed indication against the calculated takeoff data throughout the ground roll, with liftoff held within the -0,+5 knots tolerance and no acceleration overshoot. Rotation was initiated a few knots later than the briefed speed on one attempt before the cross-check tightened. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the cross-check at the same rate from brake release to rotation.

texts_above.1: SP rotated at the computed speed and controlled liftoff to about 10 knots fast, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP held liftoff to approximately 7 knots fast, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances, catching the trend from a delayed cross-check late in the ground roll and containing it without any IP intervention. Rotation and the takeoff attitude were set correctly once the trend had been recognized. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good takeoff-airspeed cross-check.
texts_above.3: SP cross-checked the airspeed indication against the calculated takeoff data from brake release to liftoff and rotated at the briefed speed with airspeed held within the -0,+5 knots tolerance on every takeoff. No acceleration overshoot developed on any attempt. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise takeoff-airspeed cross-check.
texts_above.4: SP rotated precisely at the computed speed with negligible deviation from the standard takeoff airspeed and no perceptible overshoot during the acceleration, verifying the calculated takeoff data against actual aircraft performance throughout. The airspeed cross-check ran continuously from brake release to liftoff without a gap. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional takeoff-airspeed cross-check.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline tracking during takeoff roll
error_modes.source: specific:Maintain in the center line of RWY (ft)

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient and late rudder input against the crosswind component, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Lateral displacement exceeded 10 ft from the runway centerline, outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and continued to diverge through liftoff. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the takeoff track along the centerline.
texts.1: SP, due to directional corrections applied only after the drift had become visible, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Displacement reached about 10 ft from the runway centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the track was recovered only after a verbal call from the IP. No anticipatory rudder input was made during the acceleration.
texts.2: SP, due to coarse rudder inputs made after the drift developed rather than as it began, did not hold the A/C precisely on the centerline during the takeoff roll. Displacement reached approximately 8 ft, between the +/-5 ft and the +/-10 ft tolerances. SP identified the divergence, applied the correct rudder and re-established the track before liftoff without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during T/O, tracking within +/-5 ft from brake release to liftoff. Rudder inputs were small, anticipatory and matched to the crosswind component, and the aircraft was flown off with no lateral divergence. Directional control was maintained without any assistance from the IP.
texts.4: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during T/O with negligible lateral displacement throughout the ground roll and at liftoff. Rudder inputs anticipated the crosswind and the yaw from power application, so no correcting input larger than trim-level was required. The takeoff track remained aligned with the runway centerline into the climb.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline within the required tolerance, but the aircraft drifted repeatedly to the same side of the runway centerline and every correction was reactive rather than anticipatory. All displacements remained inside +/-5 ft and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to lead the crosswind with rudder from brake release so that the drift is prevented rather than corrected.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for rudder correction as soon as a drift began, SP applied the rudder input called for through the takeoff roll. The anticipation of the yaw produced by power application has not yet been learned, so rudder is still applied on a call rather than in anticipation of the drift. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin applying anticipatory rudder as power is set without the correction being called.
texts_at.1: SP made no anticipatory rudder input during the acceleration and recovered the track only after a verbal call from the IP, with displacement reaching about 10 ft from the runway centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, because the directional corrections had been applied only after the drift was visible. The centerline was regained once the call had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the first rudder correction as the drift begins rather than after the call.
texts_at.2: SP identified a divergence from coarse rudder inputs made after the drift had developed, applied the correct rudder and re-established the track before liftoff at about 8 ft, past the desired tolerance and inside the maximum, without any IP intervention. The displacement did not grow further before the correction. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the rudder as the drift begins rather than after it develops.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during T/O, tracking within +/-5 ft from brake release to liftoff, with rudder inputs small, anticipatory and matched to the crosswind component. One correction was made a touch later than the others, though the track stayed inside the standard throughout. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to lead every correction with the same anticipation as the earliest one.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the takeoff roll and held displacement to about 10 ft from the runway centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance. That correction came after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP tracked within about 8 ft of the runway centerline, between the +/-5 ft and +/-10 ft tolerances, recognizing one coarse rudder input made after the drift had begun and correcting the track before liftoff without any IP intervention. Directional control stayed ahead of the developing drift for the rest of the roll. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound centerline tracking on the takeoff roll.
texts_above.3: SP tracked within +/-5 ft of the runway centerline from brake release to liftoff with rudder inputs small, anticipatory and matched to the crosswind component on every takeoff. No lateral divergence developed at any point of the acceleration. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed centerline tracking on the takeoff roll.
texts_above.4: SP held negligible lateral displacement throughout the ground roll and at liftoff, with rudder inputs anticipating both the crosswind and the yaw from power application so no correction larger than trim-level was ever required. The takeoff track stayed aligned with the centerline into the climb. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary centerline tracking on the takeoff roll.

error_modes.label: LINE UP checks completeness and sequence

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in which a briefed item was omitted under workload, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions and did not accomplish the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point. More than one required item was left unverified and the omission was still uncorrected after liftoff. IP intervened by directing that the checks be re-accomplished in flight before the departure was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to a lapse under the workload of the line-up sequence, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions. One required item was omitted and was recovered only after the IP prompted the check, with the takeoff roll already begun. SP had accepted the checks as complete without a verification pass.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted flow through the LINE UP checks after the takeoff clearance was received, did not complete the checks in the briefed sequence on the first pass. SP detected the skipped item without prompting, completed it before brake release and required no IP intervention. The departure was not delayed and no item entered the takeoff roll unverified.
texts.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and accomplished the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point in the departure. Each item was verified against the actual switch position and indication rather than from memory. The flow was completed inside the time available on the runway without rushing.
texts.4: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions, in the published sequence and with each item confirmed against the corresponding indication. The After Takeoff Checklist was accomplished at the correct point with no interruption to aircraft control. Checklist discipline was maintained despite the radio and traffic activity present at the time.
texts.marginal: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions, but the flow was slow and a second scan was needed before SP was satisfied that the checks were complete. All items were verified and no prompting was required. SP is expected to consolidate the check flow so that it is completed in one pass and does not compete with lineup and directional control tasks.

texts_at.2: SP detected one item skipped in the interrupted flow through the LINE UP checks and completed it before brake release on own initiative, with no IP intervention and no delay to the departure. Nothing entered the takeoff roll unverified. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. The flow ran a little slower than the traffic pace allowed, though it stayed inside the time available on the runway. The standard for the Training Section was met. texts_above.2: SP detected one item skipped by an interrupted flow through the LINE UP checks and completed it before brake release without any prompting from the IP. No item entered the takeoff roll unverified and the departure was not delayed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid LINE UP check-flow discipline.
texts_above.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions in the briefed sequence, verifying each item against the actual switch position and indication, and accomplished the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point on every departure. Checklist discipline held even with radio and traffic activity present. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate LINE UP check-flow discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions in the published sequence with each item confirmed against the corresponding indication, and accomplished the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point with no interruption to aircraft control. Nothing about the check flow was affected by radio or traffic activity. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary LINE UP check-flow discipline.

error_modes.label: Brake hold and aircraft movement during engine run-up

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient brake pressure while advancing the PCL for the engine run-up, allowed movement of the A/C during the run-up. The aircraft crept forward before the run-up indications were checked and the run-up was not accomplished from a stationary position. IP intervened by directing the power to be retarded and the aircraft stopped before the takeoff was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to brake pressure that was relaxed as attention moved to the engine indications, allowed a continuous forward creep of the A/C during the run-up. The run-up parameters were checked while the aircraft was moving, and full brake pressure was reapplied only after the IP called the movement.
texts.2: SP, due to brake pressure applied slightly after the PCL was advanced, allowed a brief forward creep at the start of the engine run-up. SP recognized the movement immediately, arrested it with prompt brake application and completed the check of the run-up indications with the aircraft stationary. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP held the brakes firmly throughout the engine run-up and did not allow any movement of the A/C. Power was set and the engine indications were checked against the calculated takeoff data with the aircraft stationary on the centerline. Brake release was made only after the run-up check was complete.
texts.4: SP held full brake pressure before advancing the PCL and did not allow any movement of the A/C during the engine run-up. The run-up indications were checked deliberately and compared with the calculated takeoff data while the aircraft remained exactly on the centerline. Brake release and power application were then made as a single smooth sequence.
texts.marginal: SP did not allow any movement of the A/C during the engine run-up, but the brake pressure applied was only just sufficient and a slight relaxation was observed as attention shifted to the engine indications. The aircraft remained stationary and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to establish and hold positive brake pressure before the PCL is advanced so that the margin does not depend on attention.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the forward creep and directing the brake pressure to reapply, SP held the brakes at the pressure called. The brake pressure needed to hold the aircraft stationary through the run-up has not yet been learned, so the pressure is still corrected on a call rather than set and held from the start. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin holding a positive brake pressure through the whole run-up without the creep being called.
texts_at.1: SP reapplied full brake pressure only after the IP called the continuous forward creep, because attention had moved to the engine indications as the PCL was advanced. The run-up parameters were re-checked correctly once the aircraft had been stopped. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold brake pressure through the whole run-up without needing the movement called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a brief forward creep at the start of the run-up, arrested it with prompt brake application and completed the check of the run-up indications with the aircraft stationary, without any IP intervention. The creep did not recur for the remainder of the check. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set brake pressure before the PCL is advanced so no creep develops.
texts_at.3: SP held the brakes firmly throughout the engine run-up and did not allow any movement of the A/C, checking the run-up indications against the calculated takeoff data with the aircraft stationary on the centerline. Brake pressure eased slightly for a moment before being firmed up again. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold a constant brake pressure through the whole check.

texts_above.1: SP held the aircraft through the engine run-up and re-established brake pressure to stop the forward creep before the run-up parameters were checked. A verbal call from the IP came before the correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP arrested a brief forward creep at the start of the run-up with prompt brake application and completed the check of the run-up indications with the aircraft stationary, without any IP intervention. No further movement developed for the rest of the check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady brake control during the engine run-up.
texts_above.3: SP held the brakes firmly throughout the engine run-up with no movement of the A/C at any point, checking the run-up indications against the calculated takeoff data with the aircraft stationary on the centerline. Brake release was made only after the check was complete on every occasion. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate brake control during the engine run-up.
texts_above.4: SP held full brake pressure before the PCL was advanced and allowed no movement of the A/C during the run-up, checking the indications deliberately against the calculated takeoff data while the aircraft remained exactly on the centerline. Brake release and power application followed as a single smooth sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior brake control during the engine run-up.

texts.0: SP, due to an imprecise pitch input at rotation and no subsequent attitude reference, did not bring and maintain the A/C to the proper T/O attitude and did not establish the proper climbing attitude. The aircraft was flown off in a shallow attitude and the airspeed increased more than 10 knots beyond the standard, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance, while the pitch continued to wander. IP intervened on the controls to set and hold the climb attitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch input that was not stabilized against the attitude reference, did not maintain the proper T/O and climbing attitude after liftoff. The attitude oscillated and the airspeed reached about 10 knots off the standard, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance. The attitude was stabilized only after repeated verbal directions from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch rate at rotation that was slightly high and then relaxed, did not hold the proper T/O attitude steady through the initial climb. The resulting airspeed excursion reached roughly 7 knots from the standard, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances. SP recognized the attitude error against the attitude reference and re-established the proper climbing attitude promptly, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP brought and maintained the A/C to the proper T/O attitude at rotation and established the proper climbing attitude immediately after liftoff. The attitude was held steady against the attitude reference and the airspeed remained within the -0,+5 knots tolerance. No pitch oscillation developed during the transition to the climb.
texts.4: SP set the proper T/O attitude with a single smooth pitch input and transitioned directly to the proper climbing attitude with no intermediate correction. The attitude was held with negligible variation and the airspeed showed negligible deviation from the standard. Trim was used so that the climb attitude was maintained with light control forces.
texts.marginal: SP brought and maintained the A/C to the proper T/O and climbing attitude within standards, but the attitude was set through two or three small corrections rather than in one input and remained slightly unsteady in the first seconds of the climb. All resulting airspeed deviations stayed within the standard and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to set the target attitude in a single input and trim early so that the climb attitude is stable from liftoff.

error_modes.label: Acceleration to and maintenance of standard climb airspeed

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch attitude flown without reference to the airspeed trend, did not accelerate and maintain the proper climb airspeed after the configuration was clean. The airspeed diverged more than 10 knots from the standard climb airspeed, beyond the -0,+10 knots tolerance applied to the takeoff airspeed, and the divergence persisted into the departure. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the standard climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to late and undersized pitch corrections, did not maintain the proper climb airspeed once the aircraft was clean. The airspeed settled about 10 knots off the standard climb airspeed, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance, and returned to the standard only after repeated verbal directions from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch attitude set slightly low during the acceleration, did not stabilize on the standard climb airspeed at the briefed point. The airspeed deviation reached approximately 7 knots, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances. SP identified the deviation on the airspeed indication and corrected it with a measured pitch change, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed and maintained it through the departure. Pitch was adjusted in small increments against the airspeed indication and the airspeed was held within the -0,+5 knots tolerance. Trim was set so that the airspeed remained stable without continuous control input.
texts.4: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed on schedule and maintained it with negligible deviation.
